We report a case of a 62-year-old man with diabetes who developed
progressive stiffness of the hips and legs and elevated levels of antibody to
glutamic acid decarboxylase. He had a partial response to both baclofen and
diazepam, but could not tolerate the treatment because of somnolence. He
eventually received 2 infusions of rituximab 1000 mg a week apart. The
baclofen was discontinued and the diazepam was tapered. However, 6
months after the rituximab treatment, despite continued clinical improvement
the patient had persistently elevated titers of antibody to glutamic acid
decarboxylase. We postulate that rituximab was associated with clinical
improvement through mechanisms other than antibody depletion.

CASE REPORT
A 62-year-old African-American man was referred to the
rheumatology clinic because of lower extremity weakness and
stiffness. For the past year, he has been complaining of shooting
pains and numbness of his legs with associated weakness, and was
diagnosed elsewhere as having a lumbar radiculopathy. He subse-
quently developed progressive stiffness of the hips and legs, along
with experiencing difﬁculty in getting out of a chair or turning over
in bed. The stiffness was worsened by stressful events. He had no
upper extremity pain, weakness, or stiffness. There was no joint pain
or swelling. There was no history of fevers, chills, weight loss,
photosensitive rash, Raynaud phenomenon, oral sores, dry eyes or
mouth, chest pains, dyspnea, gastrointestinal or genitourinary com-

plaints. Previous evaluation revealed elevated antinuclear antibody
(ANA) and anti-SSA/SSB titers, mildly elevated creatine kinase
levels, normal aldolase level, and an elevated thyroid stimulating
hormone level of 6.8 mIU/L (N: 0.5– 4.7). A spinal magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) revealed mild to moderate cervical and
lumbar stenosis. An electromyography performed on the right lower
extremity and lumbar paraspinal muscles was normal, even though
the patient was unable to completely relax the paraspinal muscles. A
lower extremity MRI showed normal musculature, and atrophic
changes but no inﬂammation or inclusion bodies were present in a
right thigh biopsy. He was started on a trial of prednisone 40 mg/d
with some improvement manifested as being able to get out of bed
by himself. He was also begun on levothyroxin 0.75 mg daily as a
result of which the thyroid stimulating hormone subsequently nor-
malized. His prednisone was slowly tapered to 10 mg/day. However,
he continued to have stiffness and rigidity of his legs, and fell twice
as a result of loss of balance. He was then started on 10 mg of
baclofen 3 times a day with only minimal improvement, and sub-
sequently was referred to the rheumatology clinic.
The patient had been diagnosed with diabetes 2 years ago,
which was controlled by subcutaneously administrating insulin
glargine 15 mg daily. He also suffered from hypertension. He had
benign prostatic hypertrophy and was treated by post-transurethral
resection of the prostate with multiple biopsies, which were all
negative for malignancy. He had undergone a colonoscopy 4 years
ago, which was normal. He had been smoking a pack of cigarettes
per day for 20 years but had stopped doing so from the past 20 years
or more. He denied alcohol intake or the use of illicit drugs. His
other medications included aspirin 81 mg/d, carvedilol phosphate 10
mg/d, candesartan/hydrochlorothiazide 16 mg/12.5 mg daily, and
felodipine 5 mg daily.
When seen in the clinic, he was noted to have a stiff axial
posture with rigid back and thigh musculature. He was awake, alert,
and oriented to time, place, and person. His memory was intact. The
cranial nerves were all intact. He had normal muscle strength, intact
sensory perception, 2 /H11001deep tendon reﬂexes, intact ﬁnger-to-nose
test, but a stiff gait. He had not experienced tremors. The remainder
of the physical examination was found to be normal. Laboratory
studies showed a normal complete blood count and serum chemis-
tries except for a mildly elevated glucose at 140 mg/dL. The
inﬂammatory markers were not elevated, and the creatine kinase was
mildly elevated at 268 IU/L (N: 52–200). The level of aldolase was
normal. ANA titer was 1:320 (mixed pattern) and the SSA antibody

titer was mildly elevated at 51 AU/mL (N: /H1102140). The rest of the
serologic examinations including the following tests: anti-double
stranded deoxyribonucleic acid, extractable nuclear antibody panel,
antiproteinase 3, antimyeloperoxidase, and anti-Jo1, were found to
be negative. C3 and C4 levels were normal. Chest x-ray and
computed tomography scan of the pelvis were normal. The brain
computed tomography scan and MRI were also normal.
Anti-GAD levels were elevated at 102.86 U/mL (radioimmu-
noassay method, N: 0 –1.45 U/mL; ARUP Labs, Salt Lake City,
UT). A diagnosis of SPS was made. Although he had elevated ANA
and SSA antibody titers, he had no other clinical features of systemic
lupus erythematosus, Sjogren syndrome, or any other connective
tissue disease. He was placed on diazepam 10 mg t.i.d. in addition
to baclofen, as a result of which signiﬁcant improvement was seen
in his rigidity. He was later able to ambulate without any assistance.
The prednisone dose was discontinued. However, he complained of
somnolence that signiﬁcantly hindered his ability to function inde-
pendently and also prevented dose optimization. He eventually
received 2 infusions of rituximab 1000 mg 1 week apart. His
condition continued to improve, and he was able to do his daily
activities independently. Post rituximab therapy, the anti-GAD went
down to 89.17 U/mL after 3 months. However, by the fourth month,
it had risen to more than 250 IUva/mL (enzyme-linked immunosor-
bent assay, N: 0 –5.0 IU/mL; ARUP Labs), and was maintained at a
level /H11022250 IU/mL after 6 months (Fig. 1). It should be noted that
although the tests were done in the same laboratory, the methods
used were different. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay is a newer
and simpler method, probably more speciﬁc and sensitive, and the
results obtained using this test correlate well with that of radioim-
munoassay.
8 Both these techniques are reliable, but the methods and
units used by both are different, and therefore it is not possible to
compare and trend the results. Regardless, the anti-GAD level of our
patient remained more than the reportable value (/H11022250 IU/mL), and in
spite of these elevated titers, the patient continued to improve clinically.
The baclofen has been tapered and discontinued, whereas the diazepam
has also been tapered to 10 mg twice a day.
